### #1811 worker: concurrency=4 under a 2 GiB hard limit — overlapping 1M-row suites can OOM the whole worker (beat included)
labels: bug, priority/P2
created: 2026-09-02T08:01:38Z
## Context
Found by `/code-review` on #1810 (the #1790 fix, which pins Celery concurrency to 4 — the value Azure already ran by accident and `perf-baseline.md` measured with).

## The gap
`docs/site/perf-baseline.md` measured **single-run** worker peaks of ~1.2 GiB (CSV 1M) to ~1.7 GiB (UC 1M) under the 1 CPU / 2 GiB rig. With 4 prefork children, two overlapping large suites (a schedule collision, or a manual run beside a scheduled one) can push task RSS past the 2048 MiB hard limit. ECS/ACA then OOM-kill the **whole container**, which includes the embedded beat (`worker -B`) — every periodic task stops silently, the #405 class. `worker_max_memory_per_child_kb` recycles a child *between* tasks; it does not bound concurrent peaks.

This predates #1810 on Azure (it ran 4 already) and was masked on AWS only because the unpinned default happened to be 2.

## Options (decide in W6 perf)
1. Size memory to concurrency: 4 GiB worker tasks on both clouds (cost).
2. Lower concurrency to 2 and re-baseline (`perf-baseline.md` rig changes).
3. Keep 4 but add a per-task memory guard / admission control for sampled-vs-full scans (`ScanTooLargeError` already exists for the read side; a worker-level budget does not).
4. Split beat out of the worker container so an OOM can never take the scheduler down with it.

Whatever is chosen, record the concurrent-peak measurement, not just the single-run one.

Refs: #1790, #1810, #1393 (scale baseline), #405.

### #1743 llm_invocations: unindexed JSONB scan on the alert-dispatch hot path
labels: enhancement
created: 2026-08-31T03:58:42Z
\`llm_rca.latest_narrative_for_incident\` (backend/app/services/llm_rca.py, #1647) filters \`LlmInvocation\` on \`kind\`, \`status\`, and a JSONB path expression (\`request['incident_id'].astext\`) with no supporting index. It's called once per active incident from \`_incident_cards\` (backend/app/alerting/builder.py) on **every alert-triggering run** — the alert-dispatch hot path.

As \`llm_invocations\` grows (it's a retained audit/cost record per its own docstring — see \`db/models.py\`'s \`LlmInvocation\`), a run with several simultaneously-failing checks each with an active incident triggers one effectively-unindexed scan of the whole table per incident, adding avoidable latency/DB load to alert delivery.

**Not blocking #1647** — flagged by \`/code-review\` as a real but non-urgent performance concern (LLM invocation volume is expected to stay low: manual, on-demand, cost-visible per ADR 0042), filed per CONTRIBUTING rule 3a rather than fixed inline (a new index is a migration, which the project treats as its own reviewed category — rollback plan, tested up+down).

Possible shapes to consider when picked up:
- A partial index on \`(kind, status, suite_id)\` (kind/status are already the cheap filters; \`suite_id\` is already set on every invocation at creation time and would let a suite-scoped query skip the JSONB path entirely for most of the filtering).
- A functional/GIN index on \`request\` itself if more JSONB-keyed lookups accumulate.
- Alternatively, cache the "does this incident have a narrative" lookup at incident-attach time (when \`sync_incidents_for_run\` reconciles occurrences) rather than re-querying on every alert dispatch — though this trades a write-time cost for the read-time one and needs its own design pass.

### #1715 perf(incidents): upstream-pipeline marker lookup scans PipelineRun instead of using the unique index
labels: enhancement, priority/P3
created: 2026-08-30T16:52:14Z
## Summary
`_upstream_pipeline_layer` in `backend/app/services/incident_evidence.py` (fixed in #1713 / PR #1714) resolves a run's `triggered_by` marker to its `PipelineRun` row via:

```python
func.concat(PipelineRun.provider, ":", PipelineRun.pipeline_or_dag_id, ":", PipelineRun.provider_run_id) == marker
```

scoped only by `PipelineRun.provider ==`. This is deliberate — see #1713's fix — because a plain `(provider, provider_run_id)` lookup requires correctly extracting `provider_run_id` from the marker string, and that extraction is ambiguous in general (Airflow's default `run_id` and dbt's free-form `job_name` can both contain colons, so there's no reliable split point). The `func.concat(...)` comparison sidesteps the ambiguity by reconstructing and comparing instead of parsing.

The tradeoff: `uq_pipeline_runs_provider_run` (a unique index on `(provider, provider_run_id)`) already exists and would make this an O(1) index seek, but a computed `concat()` expression can't use it — every call scans all `PipelineRun` rows for the given provider instead.

## Why this is filed, not fixed in #1714
Low severity today: this only runs once per breaching result (`incident_service.open_or_attach_incident` → `build_evidence`), not a hot request path, and DataQ is currently single-tenant at a scale where a per-provider scan is cheap. But `pipeline_runs` has no retention/purge sweep (unlike `runs`/`results`) and accumulates indefinitely at the orchestration poll cadence (10 min × N pipelines), so the cost grows unbounded over a deployment's lifetime.

## Possible directions (not decided — needs its own design pass)
- A generated/stored `marker` column on `PipelineRun`, written once at insert time (`orchestration_service.py`'s upsert) from the exact same `f"{provider}:{pipeline_or_dag_id}:{provider_run_id}"` construction already used for `Run.triggered_by`, with a matching unique index — turns the lookup back into a plain indexed equality with zero string-parsing ambiguity (the two copies are guaranteed byte-identical because they're both written from the same format string). Needs a migration + backfill.
- Alternatively, enforce a schema-level invariant that `pipeline_or_dag_id` never contains a colon (a `CHECK` constraint), which would make a simple `partition(":")`-based extraction of `provider_run_id` safe again — but this requires validating/rejecting colon-bearing dbt `job_name` values at the webhook boundary (`backend/app/orchestration/dbt.py`), which is itself an input-validation change with its own blast radius.

## Related
- #1713 (the bug this all originated from)
- PR #1714 (the fix, including the fail-closed ambiguity guard this issue's scan cost is the price of)

### #1393 perf: systematic scale baseline + regression budget (no perf regression is currently detectable)
labels: priority/P2, test
created: 2026-08-16T14:23:52Z
Carried over from the (now-retired) local `HARNESS_TODO.md` §6.

## The gap

Performance has only ever been measured **pointwise, at the moment something was fixed**:

- #327 (profiler N+1 → batched rank-join) was live-benchmarked on Snowflake and Unity Catalog pre-merge — 4.5x / 5.2x faster.
- #323 (retention-sweep index) was fixed and measured.

Both are closed, and neither left anything behind that would notice a *future* regression. There is **no baseline table and no budget**, so a change that halves run throughput ships green: nothing in CI or in the harness measures it, and the first signal would be a user noticing.

The axes below have never been measured at all.

## Headline axes

- **Run scaling** — GX run wall-clock vs **rows x checks-per-suite**, per datasource (Snowflake, UC, flat-file CSV + Parquet). Capture throughput (rows/sec) and **worker memory peak** — GX pulls the batch in-memory, so this is the likeliest cliff — and attribute time to the warehouse query vs GX itself.
- **DB growth** — p95 of `/results`, `/dashboard/summary`, `/runs` as `runs`/`results` grow past 100k rows. #323 indexed the sweep; this checks the read surface users actually wait on.
- **Profiler latency on a wide table** — now that #327 is batched, establish the post-fix number as the baseline to defend.

## Secondary axes

- **Concurrency** — N suites at once: Celery pool saturation, the 60s scheduler beat under many due schedules (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`), run-now storms → queue wait time.
- **Flat-file batch resolution at scale** — resolving the latest batch among thousands of files (list + regex cost).

## Method

- One parameterized script: datasource x volume tier x #checks → emits `(metric, value)` rows as CSV/JSON.
- Capture **app** metrics (run duration, profiler latency, API p95) *and* **resource** metrics (worker memory peak, DB CPU). The memory number is the one most likely to produce a surprise.
- Commit a **baseline table**, then a **regression budget** (fail if a tier regresses more than X% vs baseline) — the budget is the part that makes this durable rather than another one-off measurement.
- File issues for any knee found.

## Note on where this runs

The realistic axes need live Snowflake/UC, so this is harness-gated and subject to Databricks Free Edition quotas (compute pauses for the **day** if fair-use is exceeded — keep runs short and staged). The flat-file and DB-growth axes need no warehouse and can run entirely locally, so they are the cheapest place to start.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Parameterized benchmark script emitting structured `(metric, value)` output
- [ ] Baseline table committed, covering at minimum: run scaling per datasource, profiler latency on a wide table, and `/results` + `/dashboard/summary` p95 at 100k+ rows
- [ ] Worker memory peak captured alongside wall-clock for every run-scaling tier
- [ ] A regression budget defined against the baseline, with a documented way to run it
- [ ] Any knee found is filed as its own issue


### #1331 Support sampling on comparison sources — needs coherent key-set sampling, not two independent draws (#595 follow-up)
labels: enhancement
created: 2026-08-14T23:43:34Z
[#1325](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1325) (#595) added a `sampling` block to the suite run target, honoured by the flat-file and Unity Catalog **check runners**. A comparison check's `config.source` goes through the same `resolve_target`, so it *accepted* the block — and `comparison_run._source_spec` then dropped it when building the `DatasetSpec`, leaving the author with a save that looked successful and a run that materialised the whole side.

#1325 closed the honesty half: `check_service.validate_comparison_check` now **refuses** `sampling` in a comparison source with a 422 explaining why (finding C7 of the review). This issue is the capability half — actually supporting it.

## Why it is worth doing

Comparison is the one check kind that materialises **two** datasets in the worker simultaneously, which makes it the most memory-hungry path DataQ has. It is capped by `COMPARISON_MAX_ROWS` (100k per side, fail-fast), so it is not currently an OOM risk — but that cap is also the reason a large reconciliation simply cannot be run today, and sampling is the sanctioned answer everywhere else.

## The design question to settle first

A sampled comparison is **not** simply "sample both sides". The diff joins on keys, so two independent samples of 100k rows from two 5M-row datasets would share almost no keys and report ~everything as "additional in source/target" — a confidently wrong reconciliation, which is worse than refusing. Any implementation has to sample **coherently**: draw a key set, then fetch exactly those keys from both sides.

That is a genuinely different mechanism from the runner-side sampling in #595 (which draws row *positions*), which is why it was not folded in.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision recorded on coherent sampling — key-set draw, or an explicit "not supported and here is why", in ADR 0015 or beside it.
- [ ] If built: `DatasetSpec` carries the spec, both readers honour it, and **both sides' `sampling` records land on the result** (a comparison whose verdict came from a sample must say so, per #595's own AC).
- [ ] The `check_service` refusal from #1325 is lifted **only** for the shapes that are genuinely supported — a partial implementation must keep refusing the rest rather than silently ignoring it, which is the failure this whole thread exists to prevent.
- [ ] Tests cover the key-coherence property directly (two sampled sides of the same data must diff to zero mismatches, not to "everything differs").


### #1330 Reuse + simplification batch after scale-aware execution — dedupe the CSV stream construction first (#595 follow-up)
labels: chore
created: 2026-08-14T23:43:09Z
The `/code-review` fan-out on [#1325](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1325) (scale-aware execution, #595) flagged a **reuse + simplification batch** as structural follow-up. None of it is a correctness defect today; the reason to track it is that several items are *near-duplicates that must agree*, and near-duplicates that must agree are how this repo has repeatedly shipped quiet wrong answers (#476's fold, #936's quoting, #1230's write/read key pair).

## Reuse — pairs that must not drift

1. **`flatfile.object_size` vs `file_stat`.** `file_stat` returns the size too, so `object_size` is now a narrower second call to the same store API. One should be defined in terms of the other.

2. **`read_csv_head` vs `_csv_head_frame`.** Same job at two scales (a fixed window vs a growing one), and #1325 already had to fix the same quote-awareness defect in both. That is the warning shot: the next fix to one will miss the other.

3. **The CSV stream is constructed twice — and this one borders correctness.** `csv_row_count` and `_open_batch_stream` each build their own `pv.open_csv` with their own `ParseOptions`. A random sample counts with the first and takes with the second, so **any drift between the two parse configurations makes the drawn positions refer to a different row numbering than the one being walked** — an off-by-N sample with no symptom. Verified consistent at HEAD by the review; it is consistency by coincidence, not by construction. One shared constructor removes the class.

4. **The UC cap probe vs `dataset_reader`'s ADR-0015 machinery.** Both do "COUNT(\*) the target, refuse over a cap"; `monitors.row_count_from_scalar` already exists for the driver-boundary normalisation (Snowflake returns `Decimal`, Databricks `int`) and the new probe does its own `int()`.

5. **`sampling._whole_number` vs `monitors._anomaly_int`.** The same bool-is-an-int / integral-float parsing rule, written twice — and the bool trap is exactly the one that would silently turn `rows: true` into a one-row sample.

6. **`sql.qualified_sql_name` vs `core_table`'s internals.** Deliberately separate (`core_table` cannot express a clause attached to the FROM item), but they now share the per-part quoting decision through `_quote_namespace_part` and could share more.

## Simplification — dead or over-general code #1325 introduced

7. **`_csv_head_frame`'s `reached_eof` branch is partly dead** — the loop only exits with fewer than `limit` rows when EOF was reached, so `len(frame) if reached_eof else None` has an unreachable arm.
8. **`file_last_modified` has no production callers left** — it is a thin wrapper kept for the tests that exercise the seam directly. Either give it a caller or point those tests at `file_stat`.
9. **`_guard_object_size`'s `stat` parameter vs the `_stats` memo** — two mechanisms for "don't re-probe", where the memo alone would do.
10. **Three near-identical `enforce_*_cap` helpers** (`row`, `byte`, `sample`) differing only in noun and message.
11. **`parse_sample_spec`'s `None` branch** is reachable only from `registry._target_sampling`, which has already checked for `None`.
12. **`_load_frame`'s policy is duplicated** in the flat-file and UC runners — same three-way decision (sample / probe-and-refuse / read), written twice.
13. **`get_settings()` is read inside the datasources layer.** Everything else there takes its configuration as arguments, which is what keeps it unit-testable without env manipulation; the caps break that.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Items 1–3 collapsed to one implementation each. **Item 3 first** — it is the one with a real (if currently latent) wrong-answer mode, and it should land with a test that would fail if the two parse configurations diverged.
- [ ] Items 4–6 either shared or given a one-line comment recording why they are deliberately separate (verified-benign is a valid outcome; unexamined is not).
- [ ] Items 7–11 removed.
- [ ] Items 12–13 assessed: a decision recorded either way, since both are about layering rather than duplication and "leave it" may be right.
- [ ] No behaviour change — this batch should move zero tests, and any test that does move is evidence the refactor was not behaviour-preserving.


### #1329 Efficiency batch for the sampled read paths — single-pass CSV random, delta head fetch, shared sniff/client (#595 follow-up)
labels: enhancement
created: 2026-08-14T23:43:02Z
The `/code-review` fan-out on [#1325](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1325) (scale-aware execution, #595) flagged an **efficiency batch** as structural follow-up — none of it is a correctness defect, and none belonged in a PR already carrying eight must-fix findings. Filed together because they share one theme: the sampled read paths do more IO than they need to, and the waste is concentrated exactly where sampling is supposed to be cheap.

Ordered by how much they buy.

## 1. CSV `random` is a two-pass read; make it single-pass

`read_sampled_dataframe` counts the rows (`csv_row_count` streams the whole object through pyarrow) and then streams it a **second** time to take the drawn positions. For a CSV that is two full passes of egress for one sample.

A reservoir sample (Algorithm R, or Algorithm L for the skip-ahead variant) gets a uniform sample in **one** pass without knowing the population up front. The catch worth stating: `total_rows` on the sampling record currently comes from the counting pass and is genuinely useful — Algorithm L would still yield it (the rows walked), so the record need not get weaker.

Parquet is unaffected: its count is a footer read, not a pass.

## 2. `_csv_head_frame` re-fetches from byte 0 on every window growth

The growing-window loop re-reads `[0, window)` each time it doubles, so reaching 4 MB costs 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 MB instead of 4. Bounded (the doubling caps total work at ~2x) but avoidable: fetch only the delta and append to the buffer already held.

## 3. The delimiter sniff is its own range request

`_open_batch_stream` issues a separate `read_range` for `_SNIFF_BYTES` before opening the stream, and the stream's own first window covers those bytes anyway. Sniffing off the reader's first chunk removes one round trip per sampled CSV read.

## 4. `read_range` constructs a store client per call

Pre-existing (every `RangeReader` window builds a fresh boto3/Azure client), but #1325 made the path hot: a streamed CSV count, a growing head window and a batch scan all issue many range reads where the old code issued one download. Client construction per chunk is the kind of cost that only shows up under exactly this access pattern.

## 5. Thread the runner's `FileStat` memo into the sampled readers

`FlatFileCheckRunner._stat` already memoises the object's metadata for the run, but `read_sampled_dataframe` → `_csv_head_frame` calls `object_size` again because it is a module function with no access to the memo. One redundant HEAD per sampled CSV run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] CSV `random` samples in a single pass, with `total_rows` on the record no weaker than today (state explicitly what it means if the definition changes).
- [ ] The head-window loop fetches deltas, not the whole prefix again.
- [ ] One sniff, no separate request for it.
- [ ] Store-client construction is amortised across the range reads of one logical read.
- [ ] The sampled readers reuse the runner's already-fetched `FileStat` instead of re-probing.
- [ ] Each change is asserted **on the seam** (requests issued / bytes fetched), not on the returned frame — every one of these is invisible in the output, which is exactly why they survived review of the behaviour.

## The gap

Performance has only ever been measured **pointwise, at the moment something was fixed**:

### #1331 Support sampling on comparison sources — needs coherent key-set sampling, not two independent draws (#595 follow-up)

created: 2026-08-14T23:43:34Z
[#1325](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1325) (#595) added a `sampling` block to the suite run target, honoured by the flat-file and Unity Catalog **check runners**. A comparison check's `config.source` goes through the same `resolve_target`, so it *accepted* the block — and `comparison_run._source_spec` then dropped it when building the `DatasetSpec`, leaving the author with a save that looked successful and a run that materialised the whole side.

## Why it is worth doing

Comparison is the one check kind that materialises **two** datasets in the worker simultaneously, which makes it the most memory-hungry path DataQ has. It is capped by `COMPARISON_MAX_ROWS` (100k per side, fail-fast), so it is not currently an OOM risk — but that cap is also the reason a large reconciliation simply cannot be run today, and sampling is the sanctioned answer everywhere else.

A sampled comparison is **not** simply "sample both sides". The diff joins on keys, so two independent samples of 100k rows from two 5M-row datasets would share almost no keys and report ~everything as "additional in source/target" — a confidently wrong reconciliation, which is worse than refusing. Any implementation has to sample **coherently**: draw a key set, then fetch exactly those keys from both sides.

That is a genuinely different mechanism from the runner-side sampling in #595 (which draws row *positions*), which is why it was not folded in.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision recorded on coherent sampling — key-set draw, or an explicit "not supported and here is why", in ADR 0015 or beside it.
- [ ] If built: `DatasetSpec` carries the spec, both readers honour it, and **both sides' `sampling` records land on the result** (a comparison whose verdict came from a sample must say so, per #595's own AC).

### #1329 Efficiency batch for the sampled read paths — single-pass CSV random, delta head fetch, shared sniff/client (#595 follow-up)
labels: enhancement
created: 2026-08-14T23:43:02Z
The `/code-review` fan-out on [#1325](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1325) (scale-aware execution, #595) flagged an **efficiency batch** as structural follow-up — none of it is a correctness defect, and none belonged in a PR already carrying eight must-fix findings. Filed together because they share one theme: the sampled read paths do more IO than they need to, and the waste is concentrated exactly where sampling is supposed to be cheap.

Ordered by how much they buy.

## 1. CSV `random` is a two-pass read; make it single-pass

`read_sampled_dataframe` counts the rows (`csv_row_count` streams the whole object through pyarrow) and then streams it a **second** time to take the drawn positions. For a CSV that is two full passes of egress for one sample.

A reservoir sample (Algorithm R, or Algorithm L for the skip-ahead variant) gets a uniform sample in **one** pass without knowing the population up front. The catch worth stating: `total_rows` on the sampling record currently comes from the counting pass and is genuinely useful — Algorithm L would still yield it (the rows walked), so the record need not get weaker.

Parquet is unaffected: its count is a footer read, not a pass.

## 2. `_csv_head_frame` re-fetches from byte 0 on every window growth

The growing-window loop re-reads `[0, window)` each time it doubles, so reaching 4 MB costs 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 MB instead of 4. Bounded (the doubling caps total work at ~2x) but avoidable: fetch only the delta and append to the buffer already held.

## 3. The delimiter sniff is its own range request

`_open_batch_stream` issues a separate `read_range` for `_SNIFF_BYTES` before opening the stream, and the stream's own first window covers those bytes anyway. Sniffing off the reader's first chunk removes one round trip per sampled CSV read.

## 4. `read_range` constructs a store client per call

Pre-existing (every `RangeReader` window builds a fresh boto3/Azure client), but #1325 made the path hot: a streamed CSV count, a growing head window and a batch scan all issue many range reads where the old code issued one download. Client construction per chunk is the kind of cost that only shows up under exactly this access pattern.

## 5. Thread the runner's `FileStat` memo into the sampled readers

`FlatFileCheckRunner._stat` already memoises the object's metadata for the run, but `read_sampled_dataframe` → `_csv_head_frame` calls `object_size` again because it is a module function with no access to the memo. One redundant HEAD per sampled CSV run.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] CSV `random` samples in a single pass, with `total_rows` on the record no weaker than today (state explicitly what it means if the definition changes).
- [ ] The head-window loop fetches deltas, not the whole prefix again.
- [ ] One sniff, no separate request for it.
- [ ] Store-client construction is amortised across the range reads of one logical read.
- [ ] The sampled readers reuse the runner's already-fetched `FileStat` instead of re-probing.
- [ ] Each change is asserted **on the seam** (requests issued / bytes fetched), not on the returned frame — every one of these is invisible in the output, which is exactly why they survived review of the behaviour.

319	### #1243 Batch-target preview: unbounded sync listing + user regex matched in the API process
320	labels: bug
321	created: 2026-08-09T06:42:05Z
322	Filed from the `/code-review` pass on PR #1233 (batch-target preview, #1193). Deferred out of that PR because the fix is a design change (bounds + cancellation), not a line edit, and the endpoint is authenticated + edit-gated + rate-limited, so this is a hardening gap rather than an open door.
323	
324	## What
325	
326	`GET /api/v1/suites/{id}/batch-preview` (`preview_batch_target` in `backend/app/api/v1/suites.py`, service `run_target.preview_batch`) is a **sync** endpoint that does a **live object listing** under the caller's prefix and matches a **caller-supplied regex** against every key. Two consequences:
327	
328	1. **Thread-pool pressure.** Sync endpoints run in Starlette's bounded threadpool (40 threads by default). The listing is bounded only by `flatfile._BATCH_LISTING_MAX` (500,000 objects) with no wall-clock timeout and no cancellation. The frontend `BatchPreviewHint` auto-fires it on form mount and on every 400 ms typing pause, and it does not `AbortController`-cancel a superseded request (it only ignores the result). One author on a broad prefix can therefore hold several threads for a long time and stall every other sync endpoint in the API.
329	
330	   This differs from the run path, where the same listing happens **in the Celery worker**, and from the dry-run/profiler endpoints, which are bounded by the datasource's own query timeout rather than by an object count.
331	
332	2. **ReDoS surface moved into the API.** `run_target.resolve_target` already `re.compile`s a user pattern in the API process at save time, but *matching* it against arbitrary keys previously only ever happened in the worker. This endpoint is the first place the API process runs a user regex over attacker-influenceable input (object key names), so a catastrophic-backtracking pattern now pins an API thread instead of a worker.
333	
334	## Suggested direction
335	
336	- A wall-clock/object budget for the *preview* specifically, well below `_BATCH_LISTING_MAX` — a preview does not need to be exhaustive to be useful, and "scanned the first N and found no match" is an honest answer we can render (the honesty bar #1105 set for asset truncation).
337	- Client-side `AbortController` on supersession in `BatchPreviewHint`, so a fast typist doesn't leave N in-flight listings behind.
338	- Consider moving the preview off the sync path (or onto the worker) if the budget can't be made tight enough.
339	- Bound the regex work — a length cap on the pattern, and/or a per-key match budget.
340	
341	## Acceptance
342	
343	- A preview against a very large prefix returns within a bounded time with an honest partial answer, and cannot hold an API thread indefinitely.
344	- Superseded preview requests are cancelled client-side, not merely ignored.
345	- A pathological backtracking pattern cannot pin an API worker thread.

347	### #1236 lineage: a suspended snapshot prune has no durable, product-visible backstop — it can stay suspended indefinitely
348	labels: enhancement
349	created: 2026-08-08T23:42:28Z
350	Found by the `/code-review` pass on #1220 and deliberately deferred there (it needs a persisted marker, i.e. a migration, which #1220 explicitly has none of).
351	
352	## What
353	
354	#1220 introduced `WarehouseLineageResult.prunable`: a snapshot pull that only PARTIALLY observed current state (a tier skipped or half-traversed for a transient reason) is persisted accrete-only, with no stale-edge prune. Its module docstring promises:
355	
356	> The next clean pull prunes normally, so a genuinely removed dependency is at worst one cycle late — the cheap side of the trade.
357	
358	**Nothing enforces that a clean pull ever arrives.** Any *persistent* condition that reads as transient — a statement timeout on call 1 every cycle, a driver-shape error that `_feature_unsupported_reason`'s two narrow patterns don't match — leaves `authoritative_snapshot` False on every refresh, and `lineage_edges` accretes indefinitely with no prune. The promise degrades from "one cycle late" to "never", silently.
359	
360	(The likeliest concrete path — a confirmed per-object denial recurring every cycle — was closed inside #1220 itself: only UNCLASSIFIED failures set `prunable=False`. What is left is the genuinely-unclassifiable-but-persistent case.)
361	
362	## Current mitigation, and why it is not enough
363	
364	#1220 emits `warehouse_lineage_prune_suspended` at WARNING on every suspended cycle, so the condition is alertable in App Insights, and `lineage_degraded_reason` carries the transient tag on the connection. But:
365	
366	- `WarehouseRefreshOutcome` does not carry the suspension, so no API/UI surface can report it.
367	- Nothing records **how long** it has been suspended — an operator cannot distinguish "blipped once last night" from "has not pruned in three weeks", which is precisely the #828/#1091 class of blindness (a real problem the product reports as merely 'degraded').
368	
369	## Options (pick at design time)
370	
371	1. **Bounded suspension.** Persist `lineage_last_authoritative_refresh_at`; once it is older than `LINEAGE_STALE_AFTER_HOURS` (already defined, default 48h), prune anyway on the next successful pull — a stale-but-honest graph beats an unboundedly accreting one. Needs one nullable timestamp column.
372	2. **Report it.** Plumb the suspension (and its age) through `WarehouseRefreshOutcome` → connection state → `warehouse_lineage_status`, so the existing lineage banner says "pruning suspended since X".
373	
374	(1) and (2) are complementary; (2) alone is the honest-degradation minimum, (1) is the self-healing one.
375	
376	## AC
377	
378	- [ ] A snapshot connection whose prune has been suspended for longer than the configured threshold is either pruned anyway or visibly reported as suspended (with an age) on a product surface, not only in logs
379	- [ ] The choice is recorded in `warehouse_refresh`'s module docstring, which currently states the unenforced "at worst one cycle late" promise
380	- [ ] Test covering N consecutive partial cycles, asserting the backstop fires
